newsitem.title: BOLIVIA: Key economic facts about Bolivia.
newsitem.headline: Key economic facts about Bolivia.

text.p: The top presidential candidates in Bolivia's general election Sunday have few differences on economic policy.
They are all expected to continue the broad-based market reforms introduced in 1985 to fight annual inflation of 23,000 percent at the time.
The main element of the current government's policies has been an ambitious privatization program of the six major state-owned companies.
The state's electricity, rail, telecommunications, oil and and airline firms have all been sold. Tin smelter Empresa Metalurgica Vinto remains to be privatized.

Half the proceeds of the sales have been put in a trust fund which will be used for the payment of pensions in years to come for everyone over the age of 65. The returns on the fund's investments are paid out in full each year. This year, dividends from the fund are expected to be around $248 million.
Following is a list of specific policy positions by the candidates:
As the ruling party candidate, Duran promises to "pick the fruits" of reform, including speeding up investment to increase growth.

Banzer proposes revising the contracts of privatized firms to eliminate their monopolies in the country, a plan likely to antagonize the business community. He is emphasizing the renegotiation of the deal struck with the buyer of the railways, Chile's Cruz Blanca.
He also wants to lower the age to receive a pension to 55.
Paz Zamora wants to "Bolivianize" the privatized firms by introducing new rules on who sits on the boards of the companies. He also espouses a greater distribution of wealth.
He wants to lower the eligibility age for pensions to 60 years.
